title: Microlab M105: Budget 2.1 PC Speakers with a Subwoofer for Small Rooms
summary: The Microlab M105 is a compact 2.1 PC speaker set — two small satellites plus a 4-inch subwoofer, about 10 W RMS in total, wired 3.5 mm input. It's an inexpensive step up from laptop speakers; here's what to expect and what it lacks.
description:
## Who is it for?

- Upgrading from laptop speakers on a tight budget.
- Movies, music and casual gaming in a small room.
- People who want simple plug-and-play speakers.

## Why consider it?

- Dedicated subwoofer for fuller bass.
- Compact satellites and wooden sub cabinet.
- Simple 3.5 mm connection.

sections.title: What is the Microlab M105?
sections.content: Microlab is a long-running PC speaker brand, and the M105 is a mini 2.1 set: a small wooden subwoofer plus two satellites. Note that the M-105R and M105BT are different models (the BT adds Bluetooth), so check the exact model name when shopping.

sections.title: Design
sections.content: Microlab's spec sheet gives the subwoofer as 135 × 215 × 165 mm. The satellites are small enough to sit beside a monitor, and their cables are fixed rather than detachable, according to a published review. The 4-inch sub uses a bass reflex port; place it on a hard floor or desk for the clearest bass.

sections.title: Sound
sections.content: Listings and a published review put output at about 10 W RMS (2 × 2.5 W + 5 W) with a 40 Hz–20 kHz range. The dedicated sub gives noticeably fuller bass than laptop or basic 2.0 speakers, but 10 W suits a bedroom or desk, not a living room, and pushing it to maximum can distort. The tuning is for entertainment, not accurate monitoring. We have not measured it ourselves.

sections.title: Connectivity and controls
sections.content: There's a single 3.5 mm input — fine for PCs, laptops and phones with a headphone jack. There's no Bluetooth, USB or optical input, and only one volume knob; adjust bass with your computer's EQ or sub placement.

sections.title: Power and regional versions
sections.content: Microlab's spec sheet lists AC 220 V / 50 Hz. If you live in a 110–120 V country, buy a version sold for your region rather than an import.

sections.title: Who should buy it — and who shouldn't
sections.content: Buy it for cheap, bass-capable speakers in a small room. Skip it if you need Bluetooth, loud playback, separate bass control or accurate sound for editing — consider the Edifier MR3 for accuracy, or the M105BT if you want Bluetooth.

sections.title: Sources for this review
sections.content: Zero Technology has not used these speakers in person. This is a research roundup based on Microlab's M-105 spec sheet, E-Catalog's listing and a published review by 3DNews, checked November 2026. Output figures come from the review and catalog, as the spec sheet does not list wattage. The image comes from Microlab's documentation.

buying_advice: Cheap, simple upgrade for small rooms

faq.question: Does the Microlab M105 have Bluetooth?
faq.answer: No. The M105 is wired only; the separate M105BT model adds Bluetooth.

faq.question: Is 10 W loud enough?
faq.answer: For a bedroom or desk, yes. For a large living room, no.

faq.question: Can I adjust the bass?
faq.answer: No separate bass knob — use your computer's EQ or move the sub.

faq.question: Can it connect to a TV?
faq.answer: Yes, if the TV has a 3.5 mm headphone/line output. Optical-only TVs need a converter.

faq.question: M105 or Edifier MR3?
faq.answer: M105 for cheap, bassy entertainment; MR3 for accurate sound, Bluetooth and more inputs at a higher price.

faq.question: Will it work on 110 V power?
faq.answer: Microlab's sheet lists 220 V / 50 Hz, so buy a version made for your region.
